## Discussion

### Development of methodology

All proposed imputation methods performed comparably, and most discrepancies relative to the national reference values were consistent across methods. None of the approaches corrected the large deviation of the national recall data from FAO food availability estimates. The bootstrapping approach, however, yielded more precise estimates of uncertainty than the crude methods, a result that was consistent across spatial and temporal contexts and food groups. Uncertainty was generally higher for zones and months that required imputation, as expected, underscoring that overall uncertainty is driven more by missing data than by the choice of imputation method.

<!-- Shortcomings of all approaches? -->The proposed approach generates detailed estimates on the overall consumption statistics within a zone and across the year for each food item, which are not generally available in recall-based datasets. The relevance of the spatial context and temporal factors to food consumption patterns has been demonstrated repeatedly [@Rashid.2024; @Wang.2022]. <!-- shortcomings and future research --> The months preceding harvest, referred to as Hunger Gap, are generally understood to affect food consumption and increase food insecurity among smallholder households [@Stoudmann.2019]. An imputation of missing data representative of the spatial context while ignoring the temporal context needs to acknowledge this shortcoming (and vice-versa). Lastly, we benchmarked extrapolated annual food consumption estimates against the FAO FBS [@FAOSTAT]. This comparison highlights systematic differences between the LSMS-ISA food recall data and FAO FBS, albeit small at the daily individual level (up to 160 g per day per capita), the significance for nutrition and health outcomes deserves further assessment. <!-- Explain why the difference is so large for some food groups compared to others   -->

Based on the analysis presented here, the primary benefit of using a bootstrapping approach for extrapolating seven day food recall data to annual consumption lies in the improved precision of estimates and the ability to account for missing data. The bootstrapping approach allows for a more nuanced understanding of food consumption patterns across different zones and months, which is particularly relevant for smallholder households in Tanzania. The methodology can be applied to other datasets with similar characteristics, potentially improving the accuracy of food consumption estimates in LMICs. Notwithstanding, imputation cannot recover the information lost due to missingness, especially in month with very low data points. 

### Comparison of consumption estimates

The comparison of consumption estimates from the agricultural and household questionnaire (combined with the bootstrapping approach), showed a misalignment between the two sources of data. The agricultural questionnaire provided generally higher estimates for cereals & cereal products, and fruits while the recall data and bootstrapping approach provided higher estimates for starchy roots, tubers & bananas, vegetables & vegetable products, meat, poultry & eggs. Either direction is to some degree to be explained by over- and underreporting of production and consumption in the respective survey sections, as well as a misreporting of food allocation and source. The mismatch clearly highlights the importance of considering both consumption estimates to provide a more accurate assessment of food consumption and food sourcing patterns among food producing households. Assessing the degree of error in recall-based estimates depends on many factors such as recall length, survey design, item recalled and literacy level, to name a few. A study on farm labour estimates a recall error of 30-50% depending on recall length and survey design [@Arthi.2018]. A relatively common estimate of measurement error for agricultural production is 20-30% [@Wollburg.2020; @Carletto.2013]. On the consumption side, the error for food recall reported to be 10-30% in a multi-country study including Tanzania [@Beegle.2012], and 15-25% in another study with a 30-day recall [@Smith.2006]. 

<!--consumption exceeds agriculture: the case of vegetables-->Similar to the comparison to the FAO FBS, we compared the bootstrapped extrapolation to household reported production. This comparison was limited to food producing households and therefore a smaller sample size than for the previous section. A considerable proportion of items were reported consumed in the household survey only. Notably, vegetable production was not mentioned in the agricultural questionnaire when items were reported to have been consumed from production. One explanation of this discrepancy could be the use of homestead food production or kitchen gardens. According to some estimates about 10% of smallholder households in Tanzania also produce food in kitchen gardens where predominantly vegetables are grown by the women of the household [@Rybak.2018]. The small scale production of these vegetables may not be included in the reporting of overall household food production. Given that not only the quantities of vegetable production are mismatched but also the number of individual items, this explanation appears plausible. In absolute terms the median difference between production and consumption of vegetables amounts to just 4 kg across zones and may therefore be considered marginal and indicative of small kitchen garden production.

If the assumption holds that produce from kitchen gardens is not captured as agricultural production, the implications for food system research warrant careful consideration. This omission is particularly relevant for analyses that seek to relate food production diversity to household health outcomes. The literature on the association between food production diversity and household food consumption diversity, nutrition outcomes, and dietary adequacy has been mixed [@Sibhatu.2018]: some survey-based studies report a positive association, while others find weak or inconsistent effects. Evidence from Tanzania indicates that homestead food production, in particular, can improve household dietary diversity and child nutrition outcomes [@Sileshi.2022; @Blakstad.2022], although it also shows that training and long-term support are required to sustain these benefits [@Blakstad.2022].

<!-- inaccuracies in survey and estimates: milk, offal -->For livestock products, consumption reported also tends to exceed reported production, the explanations for these food groups is likely to differ from the mismatch in vegetables. In the case of meat, poultry and eggs some of the quantities of production for consumption are based on estimates and subject to a number of assumptions (see the Methods section, Chapter 3). This is due to the original purpose and design of the survey itself. For meat for example, neither of the survey sections provide any indication of what parts of the animal are consumed. Yet even if, as we do here, all edible components are assumed to be consumed (including blood and offal) production for consumption still is less than consumption from production. The extent of the difference however appears large when considering the relative difference (median difference of 85% in favour of consumption), in absolute terms the median difference is zero (mean difference of 300g) or ranges from a total difference 2.1 kg for poultry in the Lakes region to 300 g in favour of production for eggs in the Lakes region. Overall, consumption quantities for poultry are most often misaligned (consumption exceeding production by between 10 and 27% across zones); this could be due to recall bias based on simple miscounting or underestimating the poultry's weight at slaughter [@Ouma.2013]. The milk section in the livestock questionnaire also has several shortcomings (for the purpose of this study and beyond). First, and as previously mentioned in Chapter \@ref(chapter3), the way milking is reported does not allow for the reconstruction of lactation curves to verify the plausibility of the survey responses. Second, for processed milk the input quantities are often not reported even when final quantities of processed milk sold are. This is not a design failure as such but, because the final product is not reported it is neither possible to estimate the input quantities nor is there any possible approach to estimating how much of the processed milk and final product was used for home consumption. The qualitative misalignment for milk in favour of production may include the quantities not listed under processed milk and therefore compensate for the discrepancy in milk products.

<!-- agriculture exceeds consumption: inedible parts, cereals -->On the other hand, we also identified a substantial misalignment for cereals & cereal products where production for consumption exceeds consumption from production by a large degree. At the zone level, maize production exceeds consumption by up to fourfold (Northern Highlands) and twofold at the minimum (Lakes, Southern Highlands, and Coastal). Some of the observed differences may be explained by the stage at which the commodity’s weight is reported—whether in its raw, processed, or prepared state—and by whether inedible parts (such as peels, shells, or bones) are included or excluded. The food _allocated_ to the household from production is likely to contain genuinely inedible, highly fibrous portions (_e.g._, the shell of nuts). The composition and condition of the food consumed at the household level, however are unclear but often _assumed_ to still contain inedible parts, resulting in the use of refuse factors [@Mekonnen.2021; @Bromage.2018]. If some of the difference between volumes _allocated_ and those reported _consumed_ is due to inedible parts, then the use of a further refuse factor at the consumption level reduces consumption estimates further. For example, of the harvested maize cob the edible kernels make up ~36% [@USFoods_Common_Product_Yields]. For maize, one can assume that harvest includes the entire cob, while consumption is possibly kernels only (but not necessarily so), successive subtraction would reduce the volume by almost 60%.  <!--per person food consumption estimates compared to other studies etc., @Mensah.2021 Proportion of home consumption: TBD if here or next chapter, show comparison between sources; are of purchases @Dzanku.2024share of purchases @Dzanku.2024 -->

### Estimating *waste* and system-wide material flows

Disentangling measurement error, reporting bias and waste is a complex task in particular in a landscape of data scarcity [@Affognon.2015]. Household level food waste in particular is understudied in LMICs and likely underestimated in the past [@UNEP_2024_FoodWasteIndex]. For Tanzania, at the food consumption stage, estimates of annual per person food waste range form 117-245 kg a year which outstrip the estimates provided here by far (13.2 kg per person per year) [@UNEP_2024_FoodWasteIndex].

Chapter \@ref(chapter3) showed that for crops more allocation flows were recorded than for other commodities. After conducting the mass-balance calculations, the volume of unallocated flows was smallest for cereal & cereal products, legumes & pulses and nuts & seeds. Overall, any survey will contain a degree of bias and reporting error. The MFA based on the agricultural data only (Chapter \@ref(chapter3)) and the extended MFA both show that quantities are more likely to remain unallocated (quantity produced exceeds quantity allocated across destinations) rather than missing (food quantity allocated exceeds production). The degree to which this discrepancy represents error rather than allowing for a waste assumption requires further empirical evaluation ([COVID statement](#covid)). However, given the prevalence of FLW in general, it is reasonable to assume that at least some of unallocated volumes are indeed food waste.

### Implications for research and policy

<!-- [J] This is the most important discussion in this chapter and currently far too short. I will discuss this in person but, briefly, would it be possible to show how much error in FOOD WASTE estimation can be incurred through partial use of survey data? Recall data possibly more unreliable when compared to supply estimates -->By cross-referencing the different sections of the LSMS-ISA survey, we show that considering production or consumption in isolation provides only limited and incomplete information. Several noteworthy observations follow from this finding. First, no extrapolation can compensate for missing data or reporting errors; investment in better data collection is therefore crucial. Second, some survey sections are more reliable than others, particularly with respect to reported consumption. Across the agricultural and livestock questionnaires, volumes sold are consistently recorded, whereas consumption is often incompletely or only partially captured. Records for other uses or destinations, such as gifts or losses, are rarer still. Our results illustrate this for milk and especially milk products, for which processed quantities are reported inconsistently; the adjustments applied (Chapter \@ref(chapter3)) could not fully overcome this limitation. Third and crucially, drawing on both the agricultural and household surveys is necessary to obtain a more accurate picture of food sourcing and consumption. A more realistic range of food consumption across food groups can be derived when all available consumption estimates are considered. The findings presented here imply that food consumption from own production is, at the very least, systematically underestimated, and that interpreting these data for nutrition purposes requires additional caution. A more detailed nutritional analysis is needed to elucidate the real-world implications of the volume mismatches documented here, particularly regarding the extent to which nutritional adequacy is met. Moreover, several studies apply additional refuse factors to recall data, assuming that reported volumes include inedible parts [@Mekonnen.2021]. In light of our results, such adjustments would further increase discrepancies between food allocated to the household for consumption and reported household consumption. As noted above, which parts are discarded, when, and in what quantities is not always obvious, even though some assumption is ultimately required. Beyond a more thorough understanding of the nutritional implications of the overall mismatch, this work should be extended to assess the nutrients embedded in unallocated waste flows.

Some of the above issues can only be overcome through better design of the questionnaire, at the heart of which lies consistency of the questions across survey sections. Notwithstanding, the results here show that at least some losses of produce across most food groups are likely to be substantial enough to affect smallholders’ food security. Given the negative impacts these losses represent for household well-being (economic and otherwise), a wider inclusion of production-related questions across survey sections (in particular with regards to animal products) are recommended in the future.

The implications of the findings presented here, in particular for policy, are twofold. First, when designing policies or interventions that require accurate estimates of food sourcing—such as fortification efforts—our analysis demonstrates that both production and consumption survey sections need to be considered to obtain a clearer understanding of where to target interventions most effectively. Additionally, the finding that recall-based consumption is consistently lower than what is reported in agricultural surveys has important implications for interventions and policy related to food security, as it may lead to underestimation of dietary gaps and unmet nutritional needs.

<!-- In the case of eggs, a definitive representation and assessment of how production is allocated is not possible due to the production for consumption estimate being based on the information provided in the recall survey (see Methods in Chapter \@ref(chapter3)). -->Future research, in particular with a focus on agricultural diversity, consumption diversity and nutrient adequacy should consider and cross-reference reporting across survey sections to improve the relevance of study conclusions and findings. At least in terms of production diversity, accuracy can be improved by referring to the household food recall section, while sufficiency of food supply and nutrient adequacy over the course of a year benefits from the information provided in the agricultural questionnaire. This, combined with the bootstrapping method developed herein, will hopefully contribute to further advancement of food waste research. Finally, it was outside the scope of this chapter to consider the implications for reporting of other food sources or total consumption. However, a similar approach can be taken to verify sales and purchase flows by cross-referencing with market sales, trader and retail surveys and other community-based food balance sheets. This would further our understanding of waste occurrence, food availability, access and wider food system analysis.

**Implications for research methods**

This chapter has several implications for future research. In this study, data infilling by bootstrap was chosen because it provides a non-parametric, computationally feasible middle ground without strong assumptions. While no method can overcome the shortcomings of the underlying data quality, as the chapter showed, this method is superior to simple mean scaling in terms of the error terms, and it is less computationally intensive and less assumption-heavy than regression models. Bootstrapping avoids compounding temporal noise created by simply multiplying weekly outliers, caused by festivities and special occasions among other factors. Furthermore, it preserves empirical variance and provides a plausible distribution alongside a point estimate while handling zero-inflated data. Food consumption does not follow a normal distribution, making fitting regression and imputation models more challenging. The mosaic reconstruction used here breaks the link between the item-to-item co-occurrence within a weekly consumption bundle, decoupling paired items (_e.g._ rice and beans) across resampling draws. The approach represents a methodological trade-off at the cost of meal-level dietary covariance, and short-term pairing accuracy in favour of long-term nutritional vulnerability assessments. Statistical smoothing over a full year and the law of large numbers across household strata (that comprise the baseline pool for bootstrapping) provide a more nuanced estimate of macro-level volumes and year-long nutritional risks. Using this approach allows households to be grouped based on any predefined, diet-determining characteristic to estimate the group's long-term annual nutritional vulnerability. This information is highly relevant to policymaking, and thus, similar approaches can be recommended for future survey-based work that extrapolates food consumption data to annual estimates.

For the purpose at hand, the bootstrap approach enabled quantitative alignment of the survey sections to serve as a diagnostic tool. It resulted in moderate discrepancies compared to other methods and guided future qualitative data collection. By pinpointing exactly where production and consumption data diverge, researchers can target subsequent qualitative inquiries into more specific circumstances—with regards to both external shocks and daily practices—under which losses occur between post-harvest allocation to domestic consumption. The volume missing between allocation and intake can then be linked back directly to the theoretical framework of Chapter \@ref(chapter1) and practice theory. The gap highlights household members’ choices, decisions, and abilities (agency) to maintain allocated volumes for adequate consumption, revealing the human behavioural element behind the missing food. In particular, the contrasting results between perishable foods is of interest. Fruits and vegetables account for the highest share of gift origin of all food groups whereas discrepancies in milk could merely be data artefacts due to inconsistent reporting of processing volumes or spoilage, both possibly indicating some lack of agency. Qualitative and observational data collection would be required to capture these elements and generate plausible assumptions about general practices and operating space.

Internal cross-validation conducted here goes beyond what is currently included in the enumerator instructions and data checks. The ability to cross-reference data internally within the same sample and timeframe offers a robust validation mechanism. This can reveal systematic biases and allows for immediate adjustments to survey routines, such as enumerator instructions and built-in data checks, rather than requiring entirely new sampling methods or 

**Implications for evidence-based targeting and decision-making under uncertainty**

The core implication of this chapter for policy is in the accuracy of allocation. If consumption diversity is measured without cross-referencing production data, policies such as national food fortification or school feeding programs may be targeted based on an incomplete picture of local household production and resource flows. A household may report high consumption of vegetables from own production (consumption survey) but little or no production (agricultural survey). One explanation for this misalignment is that homestead production, predominantly managed by female household members, is not captured by the agricultural module, which tends to reflect formal plot-level production reported by the primary respondent. In this case, the apparent absence of productive capacity may be a survey design artefact rather than a reflection of lived reality, with implications for interventions that risk misattributing a knowledge or capacity gap where intra-household reporting asymmetry is the more plausible explanation. Other misalignments and omissions across survey sections could also lead to misguided assumptions about food sourcing and intake. For instance, if a household appears to consume little vitamin-A-rich produce (such as eggs, based on consumption recall) but reports high production for domestic consumption (in agricultural surveys), an intervention might wastefully target them for supplements they do not actually need or, conversely, overlook households where a large proportion of production is lost before reaching the consumption stage. Policies are often informed by either the production section or the consumption section and not by both. The current analysis demonstrates that without cross-referencing sections containing the same questions, the picture tends to remain limited—particularly for interventions that rely on specific food sourcing channels, such as markets versus home production.

For policymakers, the possibility of internal cross-validation speeds up the policy process. The ultimate goal of such validation is not to force survey sections into alignment but to harness the knowledge and infer current practices across food stages and household members. Relatively expeditious internal checks can flag implausible patterns and highlight incomplete knowledge of practices before data is used for high-stake decisions, thus avoiding the long lead times of commissioning new external audits. In decision-making under uncertainty, the bootstrap approach can also provide confidence bounds. A thorough recording of what household member (or members) responded to what section would allow further inferences on household structures, knowledge and power relations. The quantitative analyses provided here describe patterns that function as essential baselines for interventions. Understanding the normal gap between production and consumption enables policymakers to distinguish genuine waste reduction from mere survey noise in future evaluations. While the quantified production-consumption gaps are powerful for targeting, caution is required when inferring causality from cross-sectional survey data (as discussed further in Chapter \@ref(chapter6)). The data reveal a gap, but not necessarily why (_e.g._, theft vs spoilage vs unreported sales), or exactly how large it is once accounting for measurement bias.

### Positioning and reflexivity

This chapter was guided by a fundamental question: 'Can we coax out more from this data?' Specifically, how far can we push secondary datasets without resorting to assumption-heavy modelling? By reconciling two distinct survey sections—the 12-month agricultural recall and the 7-day household consumption recall—I constructed a data reality that I recognise may differ from the lived reality of the household. I acknowledge that 'waste' in these models may be a measurement construct rather than a purely physical one; it is the statistical footprint of hidden social practices, from informal sharing and gifting to the specificities of food preparation and food safety.

From my perspective as a nutritionist, I am acutely aware of how widely consumption surveys are used in the field, despite universal acknowledgement of their unreliability. We know they are flawed, but we rarely know in what direction or to what degree. Furthermore, the nutrition literature often relies on constant waste factors (subtracting inedible parts and accounting for cooking loss) to adjust these figures—factors that frequently lack context-relevance. My lived experience as a chef made me deeply sceptical of these standardised factors, as they ignore the dynamic routines of the kitchen and the professionalised and socialised standards that actually dictate what is discarded.

The current use of integrated agricultural and household units in food systems research intrigued me as a potential way to solve this 'recall deadlock'. The cynical reality of the current FLW research field is that there is often an institutional comfort with inconsistent evidence and 'shaky' baselines. This chapter represents my challenge to that _status quo_. By carefully verifying internal data through bootstrapping and cross-referencing, I aimed to expose hidden practices and measurement biases that standard, unreconciled surveys fail to capture, going beyond 'waste' as a measurement unit.

## Conclusion 

In conclusion, this chapter has demonstrated the potential of bootstrapping methods to extrapolate seven-day food recall data to annual consumption estimates. Applied to LSMS-ISA survey data from Tanzania, the methodology provided a more nuanced understanding of food consumption patterns across zones and months. Comparing consumption estimates from the agricultural and household questionnaires highlighted substantial misalignment between these data sources, underscoring the importance of considering both for a more accurate assessment of food consumption and sourcing patterns among smallholder households. The waste estimates presented here and in Chapter \@ref(chapter3) are much smaller than those reported elsewhere. Although part of this difference reflects the narrower system boundaries adopted in this work (focusing solely on intra-household waste), the results should nonetheless be interpreted with caution. Future research should prioritise improved data collection and more accurate methods for capturing food waste across the household food system. Finally, this chapter has discussed the implications of these findings for research and policy, emphasising the need for better data collection and survey design to improve the accuracy of food consumption estimates in LMICs. Overall, the chapter contributes to a more detailed understanding of food consumption patterns and offers a methodological framework for future research in this area.
